How are you today?
I'm doing okay. Thanks for asking. You can call me Alex.
Okay, Alex. So, what do we have today? I see you made the appointment for lesions on your hands. Is that correct?
Yeah, I kept thinking that they would go away, but that hasn't happened so far.
Also, this isn't the first time this has happened, so I figured I should get it looked at.
Yes. So, how long has it been since this latest outbreak of lesions started?
About five days ago.
I see. Any change in diet or medication?
Yes, I took ibuprofen for a fever about 12 hours before the lesions appeared.
So you mentioned having had these lesions before. Did you also take ibuprofen before that time?
Yes, I was taking ibuprofen for three days before the lesions appeared.
And did those lesions appear on your hands as well?
Yeah, same location.
That time the lesions healed after a few weeks, but there was a little bit of a mark left.
Yes, I can see the residual hyperpigmentation.
Did the lesions hurt at all?
Yes, there is a bit of a burning sensation.
OK, have you ever had any adverse reactions to other medications?
Er, not that I can think of.
Do you think it's definitely related to the ibuprofen?
That seems like the most likely explanation. We will have to confirm but I suspect that you have
what is called a fixed drug eruption which is a common immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction
to the consumption of a variety of different medications including ibuprofen. Many patients
forget about having taken over-the-counter drugs which makes diagnosis more difficult
so it is good that you have kept track of what you have taken. It definitely makes my job easier.
Yes, I am usually quite careful about what medication I take.
So you said something about confirming the diagnosis. What would that involve?
There are two possibilities. The more invasive approach is to do a small punch biopsy to examine
the epidermis and upper dermis. This would have been the best option if you hadn't told me about
your medication history or if you had an unusual presentation. The less invasive approach is a
provocation test which would use an oral challenge to check for lesion recurrence. Since you're fairly
certain that you've only had a reaction to one medication it should be relatively easy to confirm
the medication responsible for your condition. Sounds pretty straightforward so what about
treatment? I mean, the lesions do seem to go away eventually on their own, but is there anything that
can be done to help them heal faster? Yes, since your lesions are in non-mucosal areas, we can use
a topical corticosteroid therapy, as well as an oral antihistamine, which should reduce the
burning associated with the active lesions. Also, of course, once we confirm ibuprofen as the cause
of your fixed drug eruption, we will find an alternative medication for fever management.
So, anything else I should be on the lookout for?
Yes, people with fixed drug eruptions tend to be triggered by more than one medication,
so I advise you to closely monitor how you react to any medications you take,
in particular antibiotics, NSAIDs, analgesics such as acetaminophen,
antifungal agents, uric acid reducers and omeprazole.
So this condition is definitely something I should bring up whenever I am prescribed a new medication?
Yes, that is certainly the case. It would be important information for any physician treating you.

First, we will want to get your fluid and electrolyte imbalances taken care of.
This condition is also often a sign of the condition I mentioned,
chronic cholecystitis, which we will have to consider as we decide on your treatment plan.
This condition can cause chronic inflammation and, as a result, the gallbladder could rupture,
which would be a serious medical emergency. For this reason,
removal of the gallbladder is a common course of treatment.
Okay, so what are the possible side effects of taking out my gallbladder?

Well, the name you just used for this fracture, bimaliola fracture, refers to the number of
fractures about the ankle. It is quite straightforward, but as you suspect, it is
not relevant to the mechanism of injury or treatment. Another classification that you

This is a benchmark education solution sample test paper.
Hello everyone. Thank you for attending today's introductory training in emergency radiology,
which is a subspecialty of diagnostic radiology. The target audience of today's training is for
trainee A&E physicians, as you will be the emergency radiologist link to the patient
and the one who generally refers patients to an emergency radiologist for a CT scan or MRI.
As you're all aware, emergency diagnostic radiologists are an integral part of a hospital's emergency team,
and so the better we work together, the better the outcomes we can get for our patients.
So, today we hope to give you a bit of insight into the types of conditions we can treat.
The topic of today's presentation is how to read a head CT in patients presenting with headache.

So, first of all, a thorough review of each CT slice for its anatomical landmarks should be conducted and, in addition to this, an organised search for signs of various disorders that can cause headache should be carried out.

These disorders include aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage or intracranial mass such as tumor, abscess or an intracerebral or subdural hematoma, arteriovenous malformation, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and sinusitis.
The first step in this organized search is to compare the left and right cerebral hemispheres for symmetry and to look for midline shift indicative of an intracranial mass.
A midline shift of more than 5mm will require emergency surgery, while a more conservative
approach can be taken with patients presenting with less than 5mm and who are alert and neurologically intact.
The next step is to examine the bacillus cisterns for evidence of subarachnoid hemorrhage,
which is a life-threatening type of stroke caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain.
A symptom that patients diagnosed with SAH often report is the sudden onset of the worst headache of their lives.
Treatment for SAH depends on its cause, such as a ruptured aneurysm, which would likely require surgery to stop the bleeding.
The third step is to examine the ventricles as ventricular enlargement may represent an
obstructive hydrocephalus due to a mass causing obstruction to cerebrospinal fluid, a clear
fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord.
Symptoms would include headaches, double vision and poor balance among others.
This type of problem would result in one or two ventricles becoming enlarged.
On the other hand, the enlargement of all four ventricles of the brain is associated
with SAH and meningitis or may be due to a chronic condition.
Next, it is necessary to examine the brain's parenchyma, which refers to the functional
tissue in the brain that is made up of two types of brain cells, neurons and glial cells,
for anatomical distortion that is indicative of a mass lesion, bleed or vascular malformation.
The fifth and sixth steps include the examination of the sinuses.
First, the major cerebral venous sinuses, particularly the superior sagittal sinus and transverse sinuses,
should be examined for hyperdensity, which would be indicative of thrombosis,
which is the formation of a blood clot within a blood vessel.
Next, the paranasal sinuses should be examined for signs of sinusitis,
which is the inflammation of swelling of the tissue lining the sinuses.
Symptoms of sinusitis include severe headaches and double vision.
The initial diagnostic test in the evaluation of A&E patients that present with headache
is generally a non-contrast CT.
As physicians in the A&E, you may have to make the decision to order a scan
for a patient presenting with severe headaches.
In most cases, a CT is not necessary, as the source of most headaches can be determined by a careful examination of medical history and a neurological exam.
Here are the cases in which it would be necessary to order a CT scan or an MRI for a patient presenting with severe headache.
First, if the patient is having a sudden onset of headaches or feels like something is bursting inside his or her head, a CT may be needed.
In addition, if a patient reports a change in the types of headache he or she is experiencing, especially if the patient is over the age of 50, a CT may be necessary.
Another reason to order a CT would be if the patient reports having headaches with other serious symptoms, such as loss of control, a seizure or a fit, or a change in speech or alertness.

Extract 2, questions 37 to 42
You hear an interview with a dietician about malnutrition in the elderly.
You now have 90 seconds to read questions 37 to 42.
Hello everyone, I want to welcome you all today to this interesting conversation on
tackling the wider aspects of malnutrition in the elderly.
Jasmine Patch is with us today.
Jasmine is a specialised dietitian and she is currently working on the malnutrition project for a local hospital.
Thanks very much for that introduction.
So, Jasmine, why don't you start with a bit of background about malnutrition in elderly and the project you are currently working on?
I would love to.
So, malnutrition is multifactorial and often means that dietetic interventions require a multidisciplinary approach.
In response to this, the malnutrition project was set up to help manage a caseload of housebound adults who are at risk of or have malnutrition.
So, can you tell us about a typical case to help us understand the project and its unique approach?
Yes, of course.
So I'm going to talk a bit about a case study that, whilst fictional, is based on a typical
patient seen by our team.
So Mrs Thomas was referred by a speech and language therapist for poor oral intake and
significant weight loss, over 12 kilograms in about 10 weeks.
Once we received the referral, the patient's care agency was contacted through social services.
This was so we could arrange for the dietician and carer to be at the patient's home at the same time.
So, in this type of case, what are the barriers to optimal nutritional intake?
Well, the first is a reliance on others for food and drink.
Older patients often depend on others to prepare their meals, so they do not have free access to food and drink.
Another barrier is social isolation.
In this case, the patient expressed feelings of loneliness and said that she would appreciate company while she eats.
There are other barriers related to her medical condition, such as swallowing issues and poor appetite, but the social barriers play a key role.
So, what kind of plan can be put together for elderly patients suffering from malnutrition?
In this case, we put together a plan to promote weight gain by optimising nutritional intake of calories and protein.
We also wanted to ensure that the patient was provided the appropriate texture of food, as it was something she commented on during our initial assessment.
The plan included using full fat milk to make porridge and drinks and swapping from digestive biscuits to all butter shortbread biscuits.
Another part of the plan was to offer milky pudding after meals, such as rice pudding and yoghurt.
Finally, we involved the carers by having them keep food and fluid charts.
So you mentioned at the beginning of our interview that you take a multidisciplinary approach.
How would that approach be applied in this type of situation?
Well, first of all, the patient was eating soft ready meals prior to intervention,
and during our initial assessment she said that she did not like the texture of the meal and also
that she had not had any recent choking or difficulty with swallowing during or after
eating a meal. So we worked with the speech and language therapist that originally referred us
to see if the patient could be upgraded to a more normal food texture with the objective of improving
her oral intake. We also worked with her existing social service provider to review her nutritional
needs. In particular, we requested that the carers be allowed more time to prepare lunch
during the morning visit. We also started to work with what is called a befriending service
to have someone eat meals with Mrs Thomas, which helped mood and therefore nutritional intake.
And would you say that the project has been a success so far?
Yes, I most certainly would.
In the case of Mrs Thomas, she gained about 10 kilograms in 10 weeks.
The befriending service had a huge impact on her mood and appetite.
We are still working on getting her a swallow assessment
so that she no longer has to eat the same texture modified meals that she dislikes.
Also, we're working on adjusting the dietary supplement.
she was originally prescribed. So what have you learned from this project?
Well one thing we have learned is how to follow a food first approach for weight gain as we are
working with patients who often have fixed incomes so we need to make sure our plan is cost effective.
We've also faced the challenges that come with accessing a patient's home which we have overcome
by liaising with social services, district nurses and care agencies.
That is the end of Part C.
You now have two minutes to check your answers.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
That is the end of the listening test.
